info.title: SortSwift Inventory API
info.summary: Read a seller's inventory, in aggregate or one physical row at a time.
info.description:
THIS FILE IS THE CONTRACT. It is served live from the API itself at
`GET /api/inventory/openapi.json`, and the Inventory API Access page in the
SortSwift app renders this document rather than a hand-written copy of it. If a
route changes, this file changes with it and the page follows. Nothing describing
these endpoints is written down anywhere else.

## Two grains, one credential

**The aggregate feed** (`/api-key/inventory`) returns one object per PRODUCT with a
nested stock array. It is the original endpoint and the right one for
reconciliation, valuation, and anything that thinks in SKUs and quantities.

**The RAW card routes** (`/api-key/raw-cards`) return one object per STOCK ROW,
addressed by a stable immutable id, with a reserve / commit / release / return
lifecycle. They are for a system that has to track and allocate individual copies.

Both use the same Inventory API key and the same entitlement. Read the RAW card
section below before you build against it: a stock row is not always one card.

## The sandbox

**There is no separate sandbox host and no separate set of routes.** A sandbox key
(`ss_inv_sbx_...`) is the same credential shape against the same base URL, and every
route in this document already serves sandbox data when you send one. You change one
header value, not your code.

That is deliberate rather than lazy. A mock server is a second implementation of this
API, and a second implementation drifts: it would answer the reserve/commit race
differently, it would not have the real unique index behind `Idempotency-Key`, and
the first time your integration hit a genuine `version_conflict` would be in
production. With a sandbox key you are running the real controllers, the real
transactions and the real constraints against inventory nobody owns.

**What a sandbox key reaches.** Its own private tenant, seeded with ten RAW cards
covering the cases you need, two of them carrying sample card scans (see
`GET /api-key/sandbox`). It cannot see, and cannot
be pointed at, any seller's real inventory. Nothing you do with it - reserve, commit,
return, attach a barcode, reset - touches a real account.

**The two things a sandbox has that production does not** are
`POST /api-key/sandbox/reset`, which puts the fixture back so your suite can run
twice, and `/api-key/sandbox/webhooks`, which lets you register a receiver and get a
signing secret without asking anyone. A live key calling either gets `sandbox_only`.

**Both directions are covered.** The inbound receiver at `POST /webhooks/inbound` -
the one route on this API that mutates stock - accepts a sandbox key as well, scoped
to your tenant. So `order.created` deducts from your fixture and `inventory.adjust`
moves it, and a reset puts it back. Note that receiver lives on a different host; its
own section below says which.

**A sandbox key needs the same Inventory API Access subscription a live key does.**
The sandbox is part of that product, not a free trial of it. The entitlement is
re-checked on every request against the account the key belongs to, so a key stops
working the moment that subscription lapses - the same rule, and the same product
list, as a live key.

If you are integrating on behalf of a seller, the sandbox key is issued against
THEIR account and it is their subscription that keeps it alive.

**What is NOT simulated.** Nothing in the sandbox pushes to eBay, Shopify, Square or
TCGplayer, because a sandbox tenant holds no marketplace credentials. If your flow
depends on watching a card disappear from a marketplace, that part has to be tested
against a real account. Everything on THIS API behaves identically.

A seller with Inventory API Access generates one from Integrations → Inventory API
Access; if you are integrating on their behalf, ask them for it, or ask your SortSwift
contact to issue one against their account.

## Read this section before you model anything

**A RAW card is not always one physical card.** Its `id` is derived from
`stock._id`, a real ObjectId SortSwift already mints, never reuses and never
re-keys. What that row represents depends on how it was created:

- Rows created by the **scanner** are one-per-physical-card in practice. The
  Add Stock match key includes the row's own scan images, and every scan
  produces a distinct one, so scanning a card five times produces five rows at
  quantity 1 each.
- Rows created by **CSV import, manual entry, buylist intake or POS trade-in**
  are LOTS. Five identical cards entered by hand are one row at quantity 5.

So `quantity` is on every object and it is load-bearing. If your model assumes
one record equals one card, it will be wrong for the second group. Either carry
our `quantity` through, or filter to `quantity == 1` and accept that you are not
seeing everything.

## Card images: the seller's scans, catalog art as a backup, and you host them

Every RAW card carries three image slots.

- `images.front` and `images.back` are the photographs the seller took of THAT copy.
  A side they never photographed is `null`. How many rows carry one depends entirely
  on how the seller works. Scanner-created rows usually have a front, and a back
  only when the seller scans backs. Rows entered by hand, CSV or buylist usually
  have neither.
- `images.catalog` is our catalog art for the card, the backup for a row with no
  scan. It is matched to the row the way the SortSwift app matches it: the render
  for this printing where the usual render shows a different printing, else the
  render for this language, else the card's default render. `match` tells you which
  (`printing`, `language` or `default`). It is `null` when we hold no art for the
  product.

**The two kinds never mix.** A scan slot only ever holds a photo of the copy, and
catalog art only ever arrives in `images.catalog`. So you can always tell a picture
of the card in the bin from a stock picture of the card.

**Copy every image into your own storage and serve it from there.** These URLs
point at SortSwift's CDN. They are provided so you can take a copy, not so your
pages or apps can load them from us, and that is a condition of using them. It is
also the only approach that keeps working. A URL names one photograph and its
content never changes, but when a seller replaces a photo the row gets a NEW URL
and the old file can be deleted, so a hotlinked image eventually breaks. Copy a URL
the first time you see it, and copy again whenever `images.front.url` or
`images.back.url` changes. A changed photo moves the row's `updatedAt`, so an
incremental sync on `updatedAfter` already sees it.

**In the sandbox**, two of the sample cards carry scans so you can build against
these fields before you hold a live key: one has both a front and a back, one has a
front only, and a third deliberately has neither, which is the shape most real rows
have. The pictures are obvious placeholders, not photographs of a card, and the same
copy-it-yourself condition applies to them. `images.catalog` still reads `null` on
the default fixture, because the default product ids are synthetic and we hold no art
for them - reset with ids from your own catalogue and the catalog slot fills in.
`GET /api-key/sandbox` and the reset response name the rows that carry a scan.

## What this API deliberately does not serve

**No catalogue content on the RAW card routes.** The `catalog` block is identifiers
only: `productId`, `categoryId`, `groupId`. No card name, no set name, no set
abbreviation, no game name, and certainly no rarity, card number, year or variation.

This is the point of the surface, not a gap in it. These routes are paginated and
built for bulk incremental sync, so anything on the object is not read once, it is
read for every row you hold and then kept. `productId` is the TCGplayer product id;
join on it against a catalogue you license yourself. You bring the catalogue, we tell
you what is on the shelf.

(The older aggregate feed at `/api-key/inventory` still returns product and set names,
because integrations have parsed them for years. It is not the route to build a bulk
sync on.)

**No valuation.** There is no `fmv` field and no market price. `price` is the number
the SELLER set, usually through their own autopricing rules, and this API reports what
they set. SortSwift is not valuing the card for you.

## Conventions

- Every id is a string and is never reused.
- Every timestamp is UTC ISO 8601.
- Every monetary amount is a decimal STRING with two places (`"4.25"`), never a
  float. SortSwift stores prices as numbers, so serialising them raw would hand
  you `4.249999999999999`.
- Lists use opaque cursor pagination. Never construct a cursor yourself.
- Errors use one envelope: `{ "error": { code, message, details?, requestId } }`.
  Quote the `requestId` in any support request.

Control of your own disposable tenant: put the fixture back, and point
`raw_card.updated` at a receiver you control.

sandbox key. These two are the only ones that exist solely for it, and a live key
calling either gets `sandbox_only`.

get.summary: Full or incremental inventory, grouped by product
get.description:
One object per product, each carrying its stock rows and their quantities. This
is the original Inventory API endpoint. With no `updatedSince`, `limit`, or
`cursor`, its response shape is unchanged.

### Recommended incremental mirror

Start with `updatedSince=<your last successful checkpoint>` and a `limit`.
`updatedSince` must be a real canonical UTC ISO instant, for example
`2026-09-18T19:30:00.000Z`; ambiguous dates and impossible calendar dates are
rejected with 400 rather than being widened into a full export.

The first response fixes `sync.snapshotAt`. Every opaque `nextCursor` carries
that same lower and upper bound, so inventory written while you page is deferred
to the NEXT sync rather than skipped or duplicated inside this one. Pass each
`pagination.nextCursor` back unchanged until `hasMore` is false. Only the final
page contains `sync.nextUpdatedSince`; persist that value as the next run's
`updatedSince`. Never advance your checkpoint from an intermediate page.
The snapshot deliberately trails the server clock by five seconds, so a write
already in flight cannot commit behind the checkpoint; that newest edge is
returned by the next sync.

**One-time bootstrap:** because this endpoint ignored `updatedSince` before API
version 1.5, an existing integration does not yet have a trustworthy server
checkpoint. Run one incremental walk from `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`, persist
the final `nextUpdatedSince`, then use that value for every later run. Do not use
a legacy full response's `generatedAt` as an incremental checkpoint.

Incremental pages are state-replacement records and therefore ALWAYS contain
quantity-zero rows and deletion state. `inventory[].deleted=true` with an empty
`stock` array is a product tombstone: remove the whole product. On a live product,
`stock[].deleted=true` is a row tombstone: remove that stock row. Replace every
changed product in your mirror with the complete product state returned here.
A row that sells out is a tombstone too, and so is a product whose last row sold:
to restock one later, read its ids with `includeDeleted=true`, below.
The optional `includeZeroQuantity` flag has no effect in incremental mode because
hiding a transition to zero would make convergence impossible.

**In legacy/full mode, sold-out rows are excluded by default.** Pass
`includeZeroQuantity=true` to
include rows sitting at zero, which is what you want if a row can still be live
on a marketplace at quantity 0 and a count derived from the default feed would
run short. It does not return deleted rows, and a row that sells out is usually
flagged deleted the moment it reaches zero.

**To find a row at 0 so you can restock it, pass `includeDeleted=true`.** Every
row comes back, including deleted rows and products whose every row is deleted,
each with its `inventoryId` and `stockItemId`. Send those to `inventory.adjust`
(see `/webhooks/inbound`) and the row returns at the quantity you set, counted from
0. Each product and row carries `deleted`, and each row `sellerDeleted`, which is
true for a row the seller removed rather than one that sold out; a row removed
before 14 October 2026 can read false. **Check it before you restock:** adding to a row
the seller removed brings it back too, and the change is pushed to their channels.
A deleted row always reads `quantity: 0`. Left out: a deleted product SortSwift
holds a live duplicate of, where you restock the live one instead. Use it with a
`limit`, because this is every row the seller has ever held. In incremental mode
the flag has no effect.

**Legacy full pagination is opt-in and keyset.** Supplying `limit` or its legacy
cursor without `updatedSince` engages it;
without either you get the whole catalogue in one response, which is what every
existing integration reads. The cursor is the `inventoryId` of the last row of
the previous page, so a page boundary cannot shift under a concurrent write.
Keep going until `pagination.hasMore` is false.

**Above roughly 15,000 products you must paginate.** The unpaginated response
becomes too large to return at all, and the failure is not obvious from the
outside: it surfaces as a 504 rather than as anything naming size. `limit`
accepts 1 to 5000 and defaults to 1000.

**The unpaginated response is cached for five minutes** per seller, and the
cache is invalidated by any change to that seller's inventory: a cached response
is only served while the inventory is unchanged since it was built, so a write
is never hidden behind it.
`cached`, `generatedAt` and `expiresAt` tell you which you got. Paginated,
`includeZeroQuantity` and `includeDeleted` responses are never cached, because the cache holds one
payload per seller and storing a variant there would serve it to the next caller
asking for something else.

Note this endpoint's error shape is `{ success: false, error }`, not the
`{ error: { code, ... } }` envelope the RAW card routes use. Existing
integrations parse the former and it is not going to change under them.

parameters.name: includeZeroQuantity
parameters.description:
Include rows at quantity 0 that are not flagged deleted. A row that sells out
is usually flagged deleted: to get those, use `includeDeleted`.

parameters.name: includeDeleted
parameters.description:
Return every row, deleted ones and deleted products too, flagged, so you can
find a row at 0 and restock it. Implies `includeZeroQuantity`.

parameters.name: updatedSince
parameters.description:
Start an incremental sync strictly after this canonical UTC ISO instant.
Omit it on later pages if you pass the opaque incremental cursor; the cursor
already binds the original lower bound and snapshot.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description:
The `pagination.nextCursor` from the previous page. Incremental cursors are
opaque and snapshot-bound; pass them back verbatim and never construct one.

200.description: The seller's inventory.

cached.description: Whether this came from the five minute cache.

includeDeleted.description: Present and true for incremental responses, and when you passed `includeDeleted=true`.

nextUpdatedSince.description: Null until the final page; persist the final value.

pagination.description: Present only when pagination was engaged.

get.description:
The sales the seller set up under Scheduled Sales, read-only. Each sale carries
its name, its discount, its start and end, what it applies to, and whether it is
on now. This is what an in-store screen or a website banner reads to show the
current deals without anyone retyping them.

**`active` is the one field to trust for "on sale now".** It is true while the
sale's price is on the stock rows it reaches. A sale becomes active shortly after
its `startsAt`, once its price has been written to every row it matched, and stops
being active at its `endsAt` or when the seller cancels it. Do not compare
`startsAt` and `endsAt` with your own clock instead: the sale can still be
`scheduled` for a minute after it starts, and a cancelled sale keeps its end date.

**What a sale applies to.** `scope` says what the seller chose: a list of products
(`type: product`, `ids` are productIds), sets (`group` or `subgroup`, `ids` are
groupIds), or whole games (`category`, `ids` are categoryIds), optionally limited
to singles or sealed by `productKind`. While the sale is active,
`GET /api-key/sales/{saleId}/items` lists every stock row it priced, with the sale
price. A scheduled sale has no items yet: which rows it reaches, and at what price,
is decided when it starts.

**The discount.** `percent` takes `value` percent off, `amount` takes `value` off
in the store's currency, and `fixed_price` sells every row at `value`. Money here is
a plain number in the store's currency, as `/api-key/inventory` returns it.

By default only `scheduled` and `active` sales are returned. Ask for others with
`status`. Paginated in `saleId` order; keep passing `pagination.nextCursor` back
until `hasMore` is false.

Errors use the `{ success: false, error }` shape of `/api-key/inventory`.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description:
A comma list of `scheduled`, `active`, `ended`, `cancelled`, or `all`. An
unknown status is refused with 400.

200.description: The store's sales.

statuses.description: The statuses this response was filtered to.

get.summary: The stock rows an active sale has priced
get.description:
Every stock row the sale put its price on, with the sale price, while the sale is
active. `inventoryId`, `stockItemId` and `skuId` are the same ids
`/api-key/inventory` returns, so a row here joins straight onto your copy of the
inventory.

A sale that is not active (`scheduled`, `ended`, `cancelled`) returns its `sale`
and an empty `items` list. A sale with `includeNewStock` gains rows while it runs,
as matching stock is added. A row the seller has since deleted is left out.

`salePrice` is what the sale set the row to. `overridePrice` is the row's price
now, which is the sale price unless the seller changed that row by hand during the
sale; the row sells at `overridePrice`.

A `saleId` that is not one of this store's sales answers 404. Paginated in the
order the rows were priced; keep passing `pagination.nextCursor` back until
`hasMore` is false. A page can hold fewer than `limit` items when a deleted row
was left out, so read `hasMore`, not the page length.

200.description: The sale and one page of its rows.

400.description: A `saleId` that is not a sale id.

404.description: This store has no sale with that id.

post.summary: Push an event from your system into SortSwift
post.description:
The other direction: your integration POSTs to us, the same way every
marketplace adapter posts orders in.

**This is the route that MUTATES STOCK**, and it is deliberately the only one.
The RAW card PATCH writes your identifiers and nothing else, because stock
movement should go through the path that already has the validation, the audit
logging and the marketplace fan-out rather than a second thinner one beside it.

Authenticated with the same Inventory API key, entitlement re-checked per
request so a lapsed subscription stops accepting pushes immediately rather than
waiting for someone to revoke the key. Rate limited per key, and failing
closed: a Redis outage throttles rather than waving traffic through, because
this is a public credentialed surface that changes inventory.

**A SANDBOX KEY WORKS HERE TOO**, under the same entitlement as a live one.
Pushes are scoped to your sandbox tenant, so `order.created` deducts from your
fixture and `inventory.adjust` moves it. This is the route to test your intake
against before you point it at a real store, and `POST /api-key/sandbox/reset`
puts the fixture back afterwards.

**`order.created` records a sale and deducts for it. Every line comes back with
its own result:** `deducted`, `short` (with the quantity we actually had),
`duplicate` (this line of this order was already applied) or `not_found`. So a
partial success is reported per line rather than as one overall pass or fail.

Retrying the same `externalOrderId` is SAFE. Each line is recorded once, keyed on
`externalOrderId` and `stockItemId` together, at the moment it is applied, and
that record does not expire. A retry, including two copies of one request
arriving at the same time, gets `duplicate` for every line already applied
instead of deducting a second time. A line that came back `short` is applied too
(it took what we had), so its retry is also `duplicate`. That is what makes it
correct to retry a request whose response you never saw. This route does not
read an `Idempotency-Key` header; the order and row ids are the key.

**One line per `stockItemId` in an order.** Combine quantities for the same row
into one line. An order naming the same `stockItemId` twice is refused with a
400 before anything is deducted.

**Three optional `order.created` fields decide where the order lands.** Each must
be a boolean when sent; anything else is a 400.

- `picked: true` marks every line already picked, so nothing waits in Pick &
  Pack. Send it when the order was pulled on your own system. Default `false`.
- `paid: false` files the order under Awaiting Payment. Send the same
  `order.created` again with `paid: true` once it is paid: its lines come back
  `duplicate` and the order moves to paid. Default `true`, so a resend that leaves
  `paid` out also reads paid.
- `createOrder: false` deducts the stock and writes NO order record. Use it when
  the sale already exists as an order on your Orders page, where a second record
  would duplicate it. **It does not keep the lines out of Pick & Pack**: every
  deducted line is a sale on the pull list. Send `picked: true` for that. Default
  `true`.

**The rest of an order's life, each keyed on your `externalOrderId`:**

- `order.reserved` holds the lines while your customer pays, the way a checkout
  on the seller's SortSwift store does: their other channels list the lines as
  unavailable and the register warns before selling them. Nothing is deducted.
  `holdMinutes` is a whole number from 1 to 60, default 15. Sending
  `order.reserved` again refreshes the hold and is always the whole reservation:
  a line left out of the repeat is released. All or nothing: a 409 lists the lines
  that are not available and holds nothing new. A 409 also means `order.created`
  already ran for this id.
  **Add `posCollection: true` to have a POS register collect it.** The response
  also carries `data.collectionCode`, a six-character code. Staff type it on the
  Reserved tab of any POS register in the store, the lines load into the cart, and
  the register sale deducts them and ends the hold, so **do not send `order.created`
  for that order**. Sending `order.reserved` again keeps the same code and refreshes
  it. Once a register has loaded the code, `order.reserved` and `order.created` are
  refused with a 409 carrying `data.collectionStatus`. `order.released`,
  `order.cancelled` or the hold expiring voids the code. A cart already loaded on a
  register can still be sold there. Without `posCollection`, nothing appears on a
  register.
  **To sell the lines as one item at one price, add `price` and `label`** ("Mystery
  Bin" at 30.00). The register, its customer screen and every receipt show that one
  item; the price is split across the lines, so stock, reports and tax still see each
  card. Send both or neither, in your store currency, with `posCollection: true` or
  on an order that already has an open code. It replaces `lines[].unitPrice`: sending
  both is a 400. A repeat `order.reserved` is the whole reservation, so send `price`
  and `label` on it again. A return is per card, at that card's share of the price.
  **A big order over the line limit is sent as parts**, each with its own
  `externalOrderId` and code. Staff load the first code and use Merge on the others
  to ring them as one sale.
  **To see a code was sold:** subscribe to `order.fulfilled`, which fires with
  `fulfillmentMethod: pickup` and `collectedAt` when a register sale collects it, or
  call `GET /webhooks/inbound/orders/{externalOrderId}/collection`.
- `order.created` for a reserved order takes the stock and ends the hold. The
  response carries `data.reservation: { consumed, released }`.
- `order.released` frees the reservation now. Safe to repeat: `data.released` is
  0 when nothing was held. A hold nobody releases expires on its own.
- `order.cancelled` marks the order Cancelled on the Orders page and frees any
  reservation. Its lines stay in Pick & Pack marked Cancelled, so staff put the
  cards back, and the sale stays in the seller's reports. **No stock is
  restored**: send `inventory.adjust` for that, and `data.stockRestored` is always
  false. An order sent with `createOrder: false` has no record to mark and is
  refused with a 409. An id we have never seen is a 404.
- `order.completed` says the order was picked and sent, or collected, on your own
  system. Its lines still waiting in Pick & Pack are marked picked, and the order
  is marked Shipped, or Collected for a pickup. Safe to repeat. A cancelled order
  is refused with a 409. An id we have never seen is a 404.
- `order.collection_simulated` works with a **sandbox key only**. It does what a
  register does when it sells an open code: it deducts the lines, ends the hold and
  marks the order collected, so you can test the whole flow with no register. Any
  live key is refused with a 403. An id with no code is a 404, and a code that is
  not open is a 409 carrying `data.collectionStatus`.

**`inventory.adjust` sets or moves a quantity.** Send `quantity` for an absolute
value or `delta` for a relative change. A `delta` that would take the row below
zero is refused and returns the current value rather than clamping silently.

**A row at 0 can be restocked.** It counts from 0, comes back with any listing ids
it still holds, and the change is pushed to your channels, whether it sold out or
the seller removed it. A row that sells out is flagged deleted, so read its ids
with `GET /api-key/inventory?includeDeleted=true`.

**A row whose document was replaced is refused.** If another document now holds the
card, adding to the old row is a 409 with `code: document_replaced` and nothing
changes. Send the change to a row on `data.liveInventoryId`; `data.liveStockItemIds`
lists its rows for the same SKU, and is empty if it has none. Lowering the old row
is still accepted. The same goes for the Merchant API's stock `PUT`.

**It can carry the row's cost too.** Add `cost`, what one unit cost you, in your
store currency (a number, 0 or more; 0 clears it; rounded to cents). It is written in
the same update as the quantity, so the push that quantity change starts carries it
to your channels (Shopify's Cost per item, for one). Send `cost` with no `quantity`
or `delta` to change only the cost: that moves no listing, and the cost reaches your
channels on their next push. The response echoes `cost` and says whether it changed
(`costChanged`). The same `cost` field is accepted by the Merchant API's
`PUT /api/merchant/v1/inventory/{inventoryId}/stock/{stockItemId}`.

**Note the host.** This one lives on `api.sortswift.com`, not
`inventory-api.sortswift.com` like everything else in this document.

orderCreated.summary: An order placed in your system

orderCreatedPickedUnpaid.summary: An order you already pulled, not yet paid

orderReserved.summary: Hold the lines while your customer pays

orderReservedForRegister.summary: Hold the lines and get a code a POS register collects

orderReservedForRegisterAtOnePrice.summary: Hold the lines and sell them on a register as one item at one price

orderCollectionSimulated.summary: Sandbox key only, what a register does when it sells an open code

orderCancelled.summary: You cancelled the order on your system

orderCompleted.summary: You picked and sent the order on your system

inventoryAdjust.summary: Set a stock row to an absolute quantity

inventoryAdjustDelta.summary: Move a stock row by a relative amount

inventoryAdjustWithCost.summary: Set a stock row's quantity and its unit cost together

inventoryAdjustCostOnly.summary: Change only a stock row's unit cost

200.description: Accepted and applied.

404.description:
`order.cancelled` or `order.completed` for an `externalOrderId` we have never
seen, `order.collection_simulated` for an order with no code, or
`inventory.adjust` for a stock row that does not exist.

409.description:
The event does not fit the order's current state, and nothing was changed:
`order.reserved` with lines not available (listed in `data.conflicts`) or for
an order `order.created` already ran for; `order.reserved` or `order.created`
for an order whose code a register has loaded or that a register has sold
(`data.collectionStatus` says which); `order.collection_simulated` for a code
that is not open; `order.cancelled` for an order sent
with `createOrder: false`; `order.completed` for a cancelled order; an
`inventory.adjust` delta that would take the row below zero (the current value
is in `data.quantity`); or an `inventory.adjust` add on a row whose document was
replaced (`code: document_replaced`, the live document in `data.liveInventoryId`).

servers.description: A DIFFERENT host to every other route here.

get.summary: Where a held order's collection code stands
get.description:
Read whether a code from `order.reserved` with `posCollection: true` was sold.
`collectionStatus` is `open`, `loaded` (a register has it in a cart), `collected`
(a register sold it), `released`, `expired` or `ordered` (`order.created` ran for
it). `collectionCode` is sent only while the code is open. A sandbox key reads its
sandbox orders.

200.description: The code's state.

404.description: This key's store has no code for that `externalOrderId`.

get.summary: List and incrementally synchronise RAW cards
get.description:
Returns one object per stock row, ordered by a stable compound key.

**Incremental sync.** Pass `updatedAfter` with the timestamp of your last
successful sync and page until `pagination.hasMore` is false. Store the
server's `updatedAt` values, not your own clock.

A row's `updatedAt` moves when the row is edited, when a sale or order takes
stock from it (from any channel: marketplaces, the store's own site, the till or
this API), and when such a sale is reversed. So a quantity change from a sale is
seen by `updatedAfter`. Overlapping your watermark by a few seconds is safe and
recommended: reading a row you already hold changes nothing.

**Tombstones.** By default only live rows are returned. Pass
`includeDeleted=true` (or `status=removed`) to receive rows SortSwift has
soft-deleted; a tombstone is a reduced object carrying only the ids,
`inventory.status: "removed"`, `deletedAt`, `updatedAt` and `version`.
SortSwift soft-deletes rather than removing, so tombstones do not expire.
A row of a product whose every row is deleted is not returned at all: to restock
one, read it from `GET /api-key/inventory?includeDeleted=true`.

**A row at quantity 0 that is not flagged deleted comes back** by default, with
`status: "unavailable"`. A row that sells out is usually flagged deleted when it
reaches zero, and then reads as a tombstone with `includeDeleted=true`.

parameters.name: updatedAfter
parameters.description:
Return only rows changed strictly after this instant: edited, sold from, or
had a sale reversed. Compared with each row's `updatedAt`.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: One or more RAW card ids (repeat, or comma-separate).

parameters.name: externalId
parameters.description: Your own id, as previously attached via PATCH.

parameters.name: barcode
parameters.description: Your own unit barcode, as previously attached via PATCH.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description:
Opaque. Pass back `pagination.nextCursor` verbatim. A cursor this API did
not issue is a 400, NOT a silent restart from page one - restarting would
hand you a duplicate of the whole catalogue mid-sync and look like it
worked.

200.description: A page of RAW cards.

get.summary: Resolve a unit barcode to exactly one RAW card
get.description:
Exact match on the barcode YOU attached via PATCH. SortSwift's own printed
labels encode a SKU or a bin address, both shared by every identical copy, so
they are not usable here and are not searched.

If a barcode resolves to more than one row this returns **409**, listing the
offending ids. It does not pick a winner: for a barcode scanned off a
physical sleeve, returning the wrong card is worse than returning nothing.

200.description: The single matching RAW card.

409.description: The barcode is attached to more than one row.

post.summary: Fetch up to 500 RAW cards by id
post.description:
For fanning out after a webhook and for reconciliation.

A malformed or unknown id is returned in `notFound`, never as an error: one
bad id in a batch of 500 must not cost you the other 499. Soft-deleted rows
come back in `data` as tombstones, because "this card is gone" is a more
useful answer than a silent omission.

200.description: The cards that resolved, and the ids that did not.
The RAW card, or its tombstone if it has been deleted.

patch.summary: Attach your own id and unit barcode to a RAW card
patch.description:
The ONLY write this API accepts, and it writes only your own identifiers.

It cannot change quantity, price, condition or bin, and that boundary is
deliberate. Stock mutation already has a route - `POST /api/webhooks/inbound`
on `api.sortswift.com`, type `inventory.adjust` - which goes through the same
validation, audit logging and marketplace fan-out every internal path does. A
second, thinner way to move stock would be a second place for it to go wrong.

An **unknown field is rejected**, not ignored. "The API accepted my write and
did nothing" is the most expensive kind of API bug to diagnose from outside.

**`Idempotency-Key`** (recommended on every call). Retrying with the same key
and the same body replays the original response. Reusing a key with a
DIFFERENT body is a 409. Keys are honoured for 24 hours.

**`If-Match`** (optional). Send the `version` from your last read. If the row
has moved since, you get 409 instead of overwriting. A malformed `If-Match`
is a 400 rather than being ignored - silently dropping it would turn your
concurrency guard into an unconditional overwrite.

**Uniqueness.** `externalId` and `barcode` are each unique per seller. A
value already attached to a different row is a 409 naming that row.

parameters.name: If-Match
parameters.description: The `version` from a previous read. Bare integer or quoted ETag.

externalId.description: Your id for this row. `null` clears it.

200.description: The updated RAW card, with an incremented `version`.

409.description:
Duplicate `externalId` or `barcode`, a stale `If-Match`, or an
`Idempotency-Key` reused with a different body. The `code` says which.

post.summary: Return a committed card to available inventory
post.description:
For a customer sellback, or any other reason a card comes back to the seller.

The EXISTING row is reused: quantity goes back up by one on the same
`rawCardId`, and its scans, catalog mapping and history stay attached. No
duplicate record is created. A row that was soft-deleted when it hit zero is
revived, otherwise the returned card would be invisible to every listing path.

**Send an `Idempotency-Key`.** This route ADDS stock, so a retry without one
double-restocks a card that does not exist.

200.description: The RAW card, back in stock.

post.description:
Takes one copy off the sellable pool without deducting it.

**What a reservation actually does.** It is stored as the same kind of hold the
SortSwift hosted storefront uses for a pay-in-store order, so it feeds the same
reserved-quantity figure the marketplace push adaptors already subtract. A
reserved card stops being listed on the channels that read that figure. It does
NOT vanish from the shop: the physical card is still on the shelf and a
cashier can still sell it over the counter, because a reservation is a promise
about allocation, not a lock on a physical object.

**A storefront shopper's hold blocks you, and yours blocks them.** Both are
promises against one card, so both are counted.

**Idempotency is durable here.** `externalReservationId` is stored on the
reservation, so retrying with the same value returns the same reservation
forever, not only inside the `Idempotency-Key` window. Use your own pack-item id.

**`expiresAt` is clamped**, to a minimum of one minute and a maximum of 24 hours
from now. An unbounded hold would let one integration take a seller's stock off
every marketplace indefinitely through a bug in someone else's queue. An absent
or unparseable value gives you the 15 minute default rather than an error.

externalReservationId.description: Your id for this allocation. The durable idempotency key.

200.description:
A replay. This `externalReservationId` already has a reservation, and it is
returned unchanged. Nothing was taken off the shelf a second time.

201.description: Reserved. The card immediately reads inventory.status "reserved".

409.description:
`raw_card_not_available`. The card is sold out, deleted, or every copy is
already held. `details.currentStatus` says which.

delete.description:
The card returns to the sellable pool. Quantity was never decremented by the
reservation, so nothing is restored; the card simply becomes listable again on
the next push.

Idempotent: releasing an already-released reservation succeeds and returns the
same object.

Releasing a COMMITTED reservation is refused with `reservation_not_active`. The
stock is gone, and reporting it as released would leave your ledger claiming a
card the seller no longer has. Use the return route instead.

200.description: Released.

post.summary: Commit a reservation, permanently allocating the card
post.description:
Decrements the card's quantity by one and consumes the reservation, in a single
transaction, so the card can never be both deducted and still held.

**No sales record is written**, deliberately. An allocation into your pack is not
a sale in the seller's own books, and putting it in their sales ledger would
inflate revenue they were never paid. The consequence, stated rather than
hidden: this stock movement does not appear in the seller's inventory timeline.

If the card sold elsewhere between reserving and committing, this answers
`409 raw_card_not_available` and the reservation is deliberately LEFT ACTIVE, so
you can see the card is genuinely gone rather than be told you own one that is
not there.

Idempotent: committing an already-committed reservation returns it unchanged.

200.description: Committed. The card is no longer sellable stock.

409.description:
`reservation_not_active` (already released or expired) or
`raw_card_not_available` (the card sold elsewhere first).

get.summary: What is in your sandbox, and is it the fixture these docs describe
get.description:
Your tenant id, when it was last seeded, and the RAW card id of every fixture
row. Start here: the ids it returns are the ones to put in your test fixtures.

**The ids are stable for the life of the tenant.** They survive a reset, so a
test that hardcodes `ss_raw_...` keeps working after your suite resets between
runs. They are unique to your tenant and are not shared with any other partner.

`seedVersion` against `currentSeedVersion` is the honest answer to "did the
fixture change under me". When `stale` is true, your data predates the fixture
documented here: `fixture` lists the CURRENT fixture, so it can name a row your
tenant does not hold yet (fetching it returns 404), and a reset adds it. A reset
never changes the id of a row you already hold; `seedVersion` moving does not
move any id.

Requires a SANDBOX key. A live key gets `403 sandbox_only`.

200.description: The tenant and its fixture.

fixture.note: Ungraded, available, quantity 1. Shares a groupId with raw-lp at a different condition.
quantity > 1. One row, six physical cards.
A slab in the shape SortSwift stores today: the grade is the condition (Grade 9) and the grading company and cert sit beside it.

post.description:
Deletes every RAW card, reservation and idempotency record in your sandbox and
seeds the documented fixture again. Run it at the start of a test job.

**Your reservations and idempotency keys go too, and that is the point.** A suite
sends the same `Idempotency-Key` values on every run; if they survived a reset,
your second green run would fail with `idempotency_key_reused` for 24 hours.

**Webhook endpoints are NOT removed.** You register a receiver once, not once per
run. Delete one explicitly if you want it gone.

**RAW card ids do not change.** A reset restores the same ids, so hardcoded test
fixtures keep working.

No `Idempotency-Key` is needed or accepted: reset is convergent, so running it
twice leaves the same state as running it once.

**Rate limited far harder than the read routes** - this is the only route on the
API that deletes. Budget a couple of resets a minute, not a couple a second.

### Seeding against your own catalogue

By default the fixture carries SYNTHETIC catalog identifiers, in a reserved band
above any live TCGplayer id. They will not resolve in a real catalogue, and that
is stated rather than hoped past: it means the default sandbox exercises your
plumbing but not your catalogue join.

Pass `catalog` with three to six `{ productId, categoryId, groupId }` entries and
the fixture is rebuilt against ids you already hold, so the join is exercised
too. The fixture's guarantees still hold whichever you use: entries 1 and 2 are
the pair that ends up sharing a groupId at two different conditions.

catalog.description:
Your own catalog identifiers. Omit for the synthetic default.
Every value must be a positive integer; a float or a negative is
refused rather than coerced, because a coerced id joins to nothing
and you would be debugging your own catalogue.

200.description: Reseeded. `removed` counts what the reset deleted.

syntheticCatalog.description:
True when the fixture used our reserved synthetic ids, which will
not resolve against a real catalogue.

post.summary: Register a receiver and get its signing secret
post.description:
Points `raw_card.updated` at a URL you control and returns the HMAC signing
secret. **The secret is shown once.** Nothing stores it readably; rotate to get a
new one.

Verification is the same three lines as every other SortSwift webhook: HMAC-SHA256
over `` `${timestamp}.${rawBody}` `` with this secret, compared against
`X-SS-Signature: t=<unixSeconds>,v1=<hex>`.

**The URL is validated the same way a live seller's is**, and the guard is not
relaxed for the sandbox: public http(s) hosts only, port 80 or 443, no
credentials in the URL, and no private, loopback, link-local or cloud-metadata
address. It is re-checked at delivery time, so a DNS rebind cannot redirect a
delivery afterwards. A tunnel to your laptop works; `http://localhost` does not.

On a live key this is `403 sandbox_only`: registering a webhook against a real
store means choosing where that store's data gets POSTed, so the person who owns
the data does it, in the SortSwift app.

201.description: Registered. The secret is in this response and nowhere else.

example.warning: Store this signing secret now. It is not shown again - rotate to get a new one.

get.description:
Never includes the signing secret. `failureCount`, `failingSince` and
`lastError` are what to read when a delivery is not arriving. An endpoint is
auto-disabled only after 24 hours with no successful delivery and at least 3
events that failed all 8 attempts, and `disabledReason` says so.

200.description: The endpoints registered against this sandbox.

post.summary: Issue a new signing secret for one receiver
post.description:
Replaces the secret and returns the new one ONCE. The old one stops verifying
immediately, so deploy the new one before you rotate if you cannot drop
deliveries.

Rotating also clears the failure counter and re-enables the endpoint. You
normally rotate because your receiver changed, and leaving it disabled by the
failures that change caused would make the rotation look like it did nothing.
The events that failed every attempt since the last successful delivery go back
in the queue (`requeued` in the response), as they do when a receiver recovers
on its own.

200.description: Rotated. The new secret is in this response and nowhere else.

delete.description:
Removes the endpoint. A reset does NOT do this - you register a receiver once,
not once per test run - so this is the only way it goes away.

200.description: Deleted.

ApiKeyAuth.name: X-API-Key
ApiKeyAuth.description:
The seller's Inventory API key, from Integrations → Inventory API Access.
The same key that reads the aggregate export.

Entitlement is re-checked on every request against the seller's live
subscription, not against the key: if the subscription lapses, access stops
immediately rather than waiting for someone to revoke the key.

A key in a query string is NOT accepted on these routes - it would end up in
access logs, proxy logs and browser history.

### Live and sandbox keys

A LIVE key is `ss_inv_...` and reads the seller's real inventory. A SANDBOX key
is `ss_inv_sbx_...` and reads a private tenant of disposable fixture data. Same
header, same base URL, same routes.

**The prefix is there so you can tell them apart at a glance**, in a config file,
in a log line and in your own CI. It is worth asserting on: the most expensive
mistake available on this API is pointing a test suite that reserves, commits and
RESETS at a live credential.

BOTH need an active Inventory API Access subscription on the account they belong
to, re-checked on every request. The sandbox is part of that product rather than
a free trial of it, so a lapsed subscription stops both keys at the same moment.

InventoryProduct.description:
One product and the stock rows the seller holds of it. `updatedAt` and `deletedAt`
are present only in incremental responses, and `deleted` in incremental and
`includeDeleted` responses. In an incremental response a deleted product has
`deleted: true` and an empty stock array and must be removed from a mirror. With
`includeDeleted` a deleted product carries its rows, so you can restock them.

upc.description:
The product's barcode (UPC/EAN) in our catalog, as a string. `""` when our
catalog holds no code for the product, which is the case for most single
cards; sealed products are where codes are held. Always equal to `upcs[0]`.

upcs.description:
Every barcode the product answers to, `upc` first. `[]` when there is none.
A product can hold several (print runs, regions, repackagings), and these
are exactly the codes a scan resolves to this product at the SortSwift
register.

Two things to code for. A code is returned as our catalog stores it, so a
12-digit UPC-A can arrive at 13 or 14 digits with leading zeros: compare
codes with leading zeros stripped. And one code can belong to more than
one product (both artworks of an Elite Trainer Box share a barcode), so a
scanned code can match several products in your mirror.

The barcodes are catalog data. In incremental mode a product is re-sent
when the seller's stock of it changes, not when our catalog gains a code
for it, so refresh them from a full export.

updatedAt.description: Incremental mode only; the authoritative product revision.

deleted.description: Incremental and `includeDeleted` only. In incremental mode, true is a product tombstone.

deletedAt.description: Incremental mode only; populated on a product tombstone.

stockItemId.description:
The same id the RAW card routes address, minus the `ss_raw_` prefix.
This is what lets you reconcile the two grains against each other.

price.description:
A float here, unlike the RAW card routes, which serialise money as a
decimal string. This endpoint predates that convention and changing it
would break every integration currently parsing it.

remark.description:
The row's remark, the location text shown in View Stock. To change it from your
own program, send `{ "remark": "..." }` to the Merchant API's
`PUT /api/merchant/v1/inventory/{inventoryId}/stock/{stockItemId}/remark` with a
key that has the `remarks:write` scope. It saves as a dashboard edit does, on
that one row; an empty string clears it; at most 200 characters.

ebayCustomLabel.description:
The "Custom label (SKU)" on your own eBay listing, when this row was
adopted from it with eBay Import Listings. Empty for every other row.
Informational only: it is never pushed to eBay and is not how SortSwift
matches eBay sales.

certNumber.description:
A graded slab's certification number, as entered on the stock item.
Always a string. Empty for raw cards and for a slab saved without one.

gradingCompany.description:
A graded slab's grading company (PSA, BGS, CGC, or the name your store
added). Empty for raw cards and for a slab saved without one.

grade.description:
The numeric grade, taken from `condition` ("Grade 9" is "9", "Grade 9.5"
is "9.5", "Grade 10 Gem Mint" is "10"). A string so a half grade keeps
its form. Empty for raw cards. `condition` still carries the full label.

overridePrice.description:
The in-store Override (the lock icon on the stock row), or null when none
is set. It outranks `price`, the row's base price. Autopricing never
changes or clears it; with "Always Respect Price Override" on in your
autopricing range it is exactly what each channel lists. A Merchant API
key with the `prices:write` scope can set or clear it with
`PUT /api/merchant/v1/inventory/{inventoryId}/stock/{stockItemId}/price`.

updatedAt.description: Incremental mode only; the stock row's latest known revision.

deleted.description:
Incremental and `includeDeleted` only. True means the row sold out or was
removed. In incremental mode it means remove this row from a mirror.

sellerDeleted.description:
`includeDeleted` only. True when the seller removed this row rather than it
selling out, as far as we recorded: a row removed before 14 October 2026
can read false. `inventory.adjust` brings either back.

deletedAt.description: Incremental mode only; populated on a stock-row tombstone.

SandboxFixtureRow.description:
One seeded row. `slot` is its stable NAME in the fixture - the thing to key a
test on when you want "the lot row" rather than a particular id.

id.description: Stable for the life of the tenant. Survives a reset.

scans.description:
Which image slots this row populates: `front`, `back`, both, or empty for a row
with no scan. Read it here rather than inferring it from whichever row you
happened to fetch first.

note.description: What this row is FOR - which behaviour it exists to make reachable.

SandboxDescription.description:
Your tenant and the fixture currently in it.

The seeded fixture is ten rows and it is chosen, not arbitrary. Four of them are
the ordinary case: three ungraded, available, quantity-1 rows with real prices,
two of which share a `groupId` at different conditions, plus one row at
`quantity > 1` so lot handling is reachable.

The other six exist because a test environment containing only the happy path is
not a test environment. Each makes one documented behaviour provokable on demand:
two graded slabs, one per shape you will meet (`graded-grade-9`, the shape
SortSwift stores today, where `condition` is the grade, `Grade 9`; and `graded`,
an older shape stores may still hold, where `condition` reads `NM` and only
`variant.graded` marks it), a sold-out row at quantity 0, a soft-deleted
tombstone, a non-Normal printing filed in a WMS bin so `inventory.warehouse` is
populated, and a row that already carries an `externalId` and a `barcode` so you
can force `duplicate_external_id` and `duplicate_barcode` rather than meet them
for the first time in production.

`graded-grade-9` was added after the first nine rows, as `seedVersion` 2. Every
id the first nine rows had is unchanged. A sandbox seeded at `seedVersion` 1
holds nine rows and reports `stale: true` until its next reset, which adds the
tenth and moves it to 2.

stale.description:
True when your data predates the fixture documented here (`seedVersion` is
not `currentSeedVersion`), so `fixture` may list a row you do not hold yet
and a reset will add it. The honest answer to "did something change under my
suite". Ids you already hold are the same either way.

SandboxWebhookEndpoint.description: A registered receiver. Never carries the signing secret.

failureCount.description:
Failed delivery attempts since the last success. Any success resets it to
zero. It does not decide the auto-disable; `failingSince` and `deadEvents` do.

failingSince.description:
The first failure since the last success, or null while healthy. While it is
set, the endpoint's other queued deliveries wait for one paced retry instead
of each being sent.

deadEvents.description:
Events that failed all 8 attempts since the last success. The endpoint is
auto-disabled once this reaches 3 and `failingSince` is 24 hours old.

SandboxWebhookSecret.description:
The one response that ever carries a signing secret. Store it on receipt; no
later read can recover it.

requeued.description:
Rotate only. How many events that failed every attempt since the endpoint's
last successful delivery were put back in the queue. They are sent again with
the same event id, signed with the new secret.

requeueTruncated.description:
Rotate only. True when more events had failed than are re-sent at once
(1000). Re-read the fixture instead of relying on the re-sent events.

Sale.description: One of the store's Scheduled Sales. See `GET /api-key/sales`.

active.description:
True while the sale's price is on its rows. The field to use for "on sale
now"; never derive it from `startsAt` and `endsAt`.

appliedAt.description: When the sale's price went onto its rows. Null until then.

type.description:
`percent`: `value` percent off. `amount`: `value` off, in the store's
currency. `fixed_price`: every row sells at `value`.

scope.description: What the seller chose the sale to apply to.

type.description:
`product`: `ids` are productIds. `group` and `subgroup`: `ids` are
groupIds (sets). `category`: `ids` are categoryIds (games).

productKind.description: Singles only, sealed only, or both (null).

includeNewStock.description: Stock added while the sale runs joins it.

itemCount.description:
How many stock rows the sale has priced and not yet put back. 0 unless the
sale is active. `GET /api-key/sales/{saleId}/items` lists them, less any row the
seller has since deleted.

SaleItem.description: A stock row an active sale priced.

stockItemId.description: The same id `/api-key/inventory` returns for the row.

salePrice.description: The price the sale set the row to, in the store's currency.

overridePrice.description:
The row's price now, as `/api-key/inventory` returns it. It is `salePrice`
unless the seller changed the row by hand during the sale.

LegacyError.description:
The error shape of the aggregate feed. The RAW card routes use the richer
`Error` envelope below; this one is kept as it is because existing integrations
parse it.

amount.description: Decimal string, two places. Never a float.

nextCursor.description: Pass back verbatim. Null on the last page.

externalId.description: Your id, if you have attached one.

barcode.description: Your unit barcode, if you have attached one.

inventoryId.description: The parent product row, for reconciling against the aggregate export.

stockItemId.description: The stock row id `id` is derived from.

catalog.description:
IDENTIFIERS ONLY. No card name, set name, set abbreviation or game name, and
no rarity, card number, year or variation.

These routes are paginated and built for bulk sync, so a name here would not
be read once, it would be read for every row you hold and then kept. Join on
`productId` against a catalogue you license yourself.

productId.description: The TCGplayer product id. This is your join key into your own catalogue.

groupId.description:
The SET. Two copies of the same card in different conditions share
both `productId` and `groupId`.

graded.description:
Read this, not `condition`. A slab's condition is normally its grade
(`Grade 9`), but slabs stored in an older shape can still say "NM"
beside their grading company, so `condition` alone cannot tell you
whether a row is graded. The sandbox seeds one of each.

quantity.description:
HOW MANY PHYSICAL CARDS THIS ROW IS. Scanner-created rows are 1; rows from
CSV import, manual entry, buylist intake or POS trade-in can be more.

allOf.description:
THE SELLER'S OWN PRICE for this row, set by them and usually by their own
autopricing rules. There is deliberately no `fmv` or market value field:
SortSwift does not value cards for you, it reports what the seller set.

A seller can price the API channel SEPARATELY from their own shelf, so
this is not always the same number their storefront shows. `source` tells
you which one you got.

A seller can also set a minimum for the API channel. An autopriced or
internal price under it is quoted at the minimum; a price the seller typed
(`channel_override`, `override`) is quoted as typed.

source.description:
Where the number came from, highest priority first.

`channel_override` the seller typed a price for this API channel.
`override` they typed a price that applies to every channel.
`inventory_api_channel` their autopricing rules for the API channel
produced it.
`internal` they have not set up an API channel price, so this is their
internal price, which is what this API served before the channel
existed and what most sellers will show.

repricedAt.description:
When the seller's autopricer last moved this price, or null if it has
never run on this row. NOT the same as `updatedAt`, which moves on any
edit, so this is the honest answer to how fresh the number is. Always
null for a typed override, which has no reprice history.

allOf.description: The seller's acquisition cost for this lot.

status.description:
`available` has unreserved stock on the shelf. `reserved` means every
copy is held, by you or by a storefront shopper. `unavailable` is at
zero but not deleted, which is also what a committed card becomes.
`removed` is a tombstone, which is also what a row usually becomes when it
sells out.

There is no separate `sold`: a sold card reads `unavailable` or `removed`,
and inventing a state for how it got there would be a claim we cannot back.

bin.description: The scanned WMS bin if there is one, else the seller's own bin name.

reservationId.description:
YOUR live reservation on this row, if you have one. Null when the row is
free, and also null when the copies are held by somebody else, because
you cannot act on a reservation that is not yours.

reservedQuantity.description:
How many copies are promised, to anyone. Lets you tell "reserved by me"
from "reserved by the shop" without a second call.

images.description:
`front` and `back` are THE SELLER'S OWN PHOTOGRAPHS of this copy, and a side
the seller did not photograph is `null`, never a stock picture. `catalog` is
our catalog art for the card, the backup for when there is no scan, and it
only ever arrives in that slot.

Copy each file into your own storage and serve it from there; do not load
these URLs from your pages or apps. See "Card images" in the introduction.

updatedAt.description:
The last time this row changed: an edit (including yours through this API),
a sale or order that took stock from it on any channel, or the reversal of
one. This is what `updatedAfter` compares against.

restockedAt.description:
**When this id started referring to a different physical card.**

A row that sells out is kept, usually flagged deleted at quantity 0, and a later
restock of the same card revives that row rather than creating a new one.
That keeps the marketplace listing ids attached so listings stay linked and
orders keep deducting, at the cost that the id outlives the card it first
described.

`updatedAt` cannot tell you this happened, because it moves on every
reprice. This can. If it is later than when you first recorded the card, the
copy in the bin is not the copy you recorded.

version.description:
Increments on every write YOU make through this API. Use it as
`If-Match`. It deliberately does not move on internal changes, such as a
sale on another channel. Detect those with `updatedAt`, which moves on
edits, sales and reversals alike.

RawCardImage.description: One of the seller's photographs of this copy, or null when they took none.

url.description:
Names exactly one photograph, and its content never changes: a new photo
arrives as a new URL. Copy the file into your own storage; do not load it
from your pages or apps.

RawCardCatalogImage.description:
Our catalog art for this card, as a backup image. NOT a photo of this copy. It is
matched to the row the way the SortSwift app matches it, and it is `null` when we
hold no art for the product.

url.description: Copy the file into your own storage; do not load it from your pages or apps.

match.description:
Which art this is. `printing` is the render for this row's printing, where
the card's usual render shows a different printing (1st Edition vs Unlimited,
reverse holos). `language` is the render for this row's language. `default` is
the card's own catalog render: English for an English catalogue, even on a
non-English row we hold no translated art for.

externalReservationId.description: Your own id for this allocation, as supplied on create.

quantity.description: Always 1. A reservation is for one physical card.

expiresAt.description: After this instant the card returns to the pool on its own.

RawCardTombstone.description: A row SortSwift has soft-deleted. Retire your copy.

deletedAt.description:
SortSwift stores a deletion FLAG and no separate deletion timestamp, so
this is the row's last write - which is the moment it was deleted unless
something touched it afterwards.

requestId.description:
Quote this in a support request. Send your own `X-Request-Id` and we
will echo it instead.

Forbidden.description: The account has no active Inventory API Access subscription.

SandboxOnly.description:
`sandbox_only`. This route exists only for a sandbox key. A 403 rather than a
404, because the route is there and working - the CREDENTIAL is the wrong one,
and a 404 would send you looking through a changelog for something that was
never removed.

RateLimited.description:
Too many requests. Retry after the interval in `Retry-After`.

The limit is per API key and per application process. SortSwift runs this
service in a 3-instance cluster, so the effective ceiling you observe can be
up to three times the advertised one depending on how requests are spread.
Stated rather than hidden, so you can size your client against its real shape.

post.summary: One or more RAW cards changed
post.description:
Register at Integrations → Inventory API Access, or via
`POST /api/admin/merchant/webhooks` on `api.sortswift.com`. Requires the same
Inventory API Access subscription.

**Verifying the signature.** Every delivery carries

    X-SS-Signature: t=<unixSeconds>,v1=<hmacSha256Hex>

where the HMAC is computed over the literal string `${t}.${rawRequestBody}`
using the endpoint's own secret - a separate secret from your API key, shown
once at registration and rotatable. Recompute over the RAW body before any
JSON parsing, compare in constant time, and reject a `t` outside your
tolerance to defeat replay.

**Delivery is at least once.** The same `id` is reused on every retry, so
deduplicate on it. Each request times out after 10 seconds, and a failed event
is retried 8 times over about 63 minutes. While an endpoint is failing, its
other queued events wait for that retry rather than each being sent. An
endpoint is auto-disabled only after 24 hours with no successful delivery and
at least 3 events that failed all 8 attempts. Re-enable it from the same admin
routes (`POST /api/admin/merchant/webhooks/{id}/enable`): that re-queues the
events it lost since its last success (`requeued` in the response), but events
that happened while it was disabled were never queued, so re-read once after
enabling. `GET /api/admin/merchant/webhooks/{id}/deliveries` shows recent
attempts, with the HTTP code and error of each.

**This is the only RAW card event, and that is deliberate.** Declaring
`raw_card.created`, `.deleted`, `.fmv.updated` and so on would promise
detection SortSwift cannot honestly perform per-row, and you would wait
forever on events that never arrive. Instead this one event fires from the
choke point every stock mutation in SortSwift already passes through - scan,
sale deduction, CSV import, POS sale, buylist intake, autopricing reprice - 
and tells you WHICH rows to re-read.

`rawCardIds` is populated when the change came through this API and we know
the exact row. `inventoryIds` is populated when the change came from
elsewhere and we know only the product; re-read those with
`GET /api-key/raw-cards?inventoryId=<id>&updatedAfter=<your last sync>`. Both
keys are always present, so you never have to branch on which produced it.

truncated.description: The id list was capped at 500. Do a windowed read instead.

fromAnInternalChange.summary: Something moved in SortSwift, and we know only the product

fromYourOwnWrite.summary: A change you made through the API, so we know the exact row
